subcategory.intro:
You walk past a weekend market and the smell of something hot makes you stop, even though you planned to go straight home. A small food stall can begin from that moment, but the real work starts before anyone takes a bite. You need a permitted place, safe preparation, enough water and a plan for the food that does not sell. A queue in one good photograph does not tell you whether the morning paid for itself.

Choose one simple dish and one crowd you can observe. Visit the proposed spot on the same day and hour you would trade. Notice when people arrive, what they carry, where they stand and whether there is power, clean water and waste collection. Ask the organiser or local authority about permission for the space. Check the applicable FSSAI registration or licence for your temporary food operation before selling; being open only on weekends does not remove food safety duties. Learn the rules for the particular venue and food you plan to serve.

Make a small batch and measure the whole day: buying ingredients, carrying equipment, keeping food at suitable conditions, serving, cleaning and bringing leftovers home. Tell customers clearly what is in the dish and handle allergy questions honestly. A family with a child should be able to see where their food was made and how it is served. If a crowd arrives suddenly, a narrow menu helps you protect hygiene and give a calm answer.

The ten paths below have different locations and production rhythms. A morning idli table depends on early preparation; a roasted corn stand depends on weather; a runner's breakfast is tied to an event finish time. Pick a product you can make consistently and a location you can use legitimately. One safe, modest weekend teaches you more than a large launch that exhausts you.
subcategory.how_to_choose: Visit the spot first and count what you would need to carry, store and clean. If you have only a few hours, a prepared item with safe holding may suit you better than a dish assembled for each customer. If a product needs cold storage or constant heat, check whether the venue can support it. Ask the organiser about stall rent, power, water, waste and cancellation. Confirm your food registration or licence path and local permissions before taking money. Price each serving after including ingredients, packaging, travel, unsold food and the whole preparation day. Begin with a small permitted trial and watch where customers wait, ask questions or walk away.

faq.q: Does a temporary weekend stall need food registration?
faq.a: Yes, temporary food vending falls within food business requirements. Check the applicable FSSAI registration or licence for your operation and the venue's permission before selling. Local site rules may also apply.

faq.q: How do I decide how much to prepare?
faq.a: Observe the same venue and time, then start with a modest test batch. Record sales, waste and the hour demand changed. Increase only when your preparation and safe holding can keep up.

faq.q: Can I cook everything at home?
faq.a: That depends on the product, your approved food operation and how it travels and is held. Check the applicable requirements. Food that was safe when packed can become unsafe after hours in heat.

faq.q: What if rain cancels the market?
faq.a: Ask the organiser about refund or transfer terms before paying for a spot. Choose ingredients and a batch size that limit loss, but do not sell compromised leftovers later to recover money.
